content:
#1 Egbert Rijke has the following idea, and it makes me wonder.

I’ll spell it out in some detail for possible bystanders, but in the end it’s quite an immediate observation that possibly has occurred to others before. Accordingly, the answer to the question at the end might be clear to those who have thought about this before, or may in any case have been discussed elsewhere. Pointers are welcome.

 \,

Consider a knot KKK, hence the isotopy-class of an embedding of differentiable manifolds of the circle into the 3-sphere

K   ⁣:  S1↪AAAS3 . K \;\colon\; S^1 \overset{ \phantom{\mathrm{AAA}} }{\hookrightarrow} S^3 \,. K:S1↪AAA​S3.

With any choice of closed tubular neighbourhood embedding

K   ⁣:  S1×D2↪AAAAS3 \mathbf{K} \;\colon\; S^1 \times \mathbb{D}^2 \overset{\phantom{\mathrm{AAAA}}}{\hookrightarrow} S^3 K:S1×D2↪AAAA​S3

(where D2\mathbb{D}^2D2 denotes the closed 2-disk)

we get a presentation of the 3-sphere as the union of the closed solid torus with the complement of that tubular neighbourhood, hence an attaching space pushout of topological spaces of this form:

S1×S1⟶AfAS3∖Int(K)g↓(po)↓S1×D2⟶AKAS3 \begin{matrix} S^1 \times S^1 &\overset{ \phantom{A} f \phantom{A} }{\longrightarrow}& S^3 \setminus {\mathrm{Int}}(\mathbf{K}) \\ {}^{\mathllap{ g }}\Big\downarrow &{}^{(\mathrm{po})}& \Big\downarrow \\ S^1 \times \mathbb{D}^2 &\underset{ \phantom{A} \mathbf{K} \phantom{A}}{\longrightarrow}& S^3 \end{matrix} S1×S1g↓⏐​S1×D2​⟶AfA​(po)AKA⟶​​S3∖Int(K)↓⏐​S3​

Here fff and ggg denote the boundary inclusions and the right vertical map is the defining inclusion of the complement in S3S^3S3

C  ≔  S3∖Int(K) C \;\coloneqq\; S^3 \setminus {\mathrm{Int}}(\mathbf{K}) C:=S3∖Int(K)

of the interior of K\mathbf{K}K.

Since the left vertical map is manifestly a cofibration in the standard model structure on topological spaces, this exhbits a homotopy pushout of the corresponding homotopy types

S1×S1⟶AfACpr1↓(hpo)↓S1⟶AKAS3 \begin{matrix} S^1 \times S^1 &\overset{ \phantom{A} f \phantom{A} }{\longrightarrow}& C \\ {}^{\mathllap{ \mathrm{pr}_1 }}\Big\downarrow &{}^{(\mathrm{hpo})}& \Big\downarrow \\ S^1 &\underset{ \phantom{A} K \phantom{A} }{\longrightarrow}& S^3 \end{matrix} S1×S1pr1​↓⏐​S1​⟶AfA​(hpo)AKA⟶​​C↓⏐​S3​

where now the left map is equivalently the projection onto the first circle factor.

For example if KKK is the unknot then this is the familiar presentation of the 3-sphere as the join of two circles.

But we may consider the homotopical data of the second diagram in its own right:

Say that a homotopy knot is the evident equivalence class of the following data:

  1. a homotopy 1-type CCC,

  2. a map f   ⁣:  S1×S1⟶Cf \;\colon\; S^1 \times S^1 \longrightarrow Cf:S1×S1⟶C

such that

  • the homotopy pushout of fff along projection to the first factor is the 3-sphere, as in the previous diagram.

Now the above construction should define a function:

ϕ   ⁣:  Knots⟶HomotopyKnots . \phi \;\colon\; \mathrm{Knots} \longrightarrow {\mathrm{HomotopyKnots}} \,. ϕ:Knots⟶HomotopyKnots.

Question: Is ϕ\phiϕ a bijection? If not, how does it fail to be one?
subject: homotopy knots?

content: #2 Better: a homotopy 1-type C=BGC=\mathbf{B}GC=BG. And we probably want some finite presentation requirements on GGG, since we know that fundamental groups of knot complements have the Wirtinger presentation, which is finite, coming from a knot diagram. One might even get more specific with the allowable finite presentations, but this is a start.

content:
#3 Some initial thoughts on #1, without having thought about it much:

1) The story misses the concept of embeddings and of knot isotopy, so I think has little chance of being right unfortunately. That is, an equivalence of a pair of knots S1→S3S^{1} \rightarrow S^{3}S1→S3 is not just a homotopy $h : S^{1} \times I \rightarrow S^{3]$ but a homotopy such that h(−,t)h(-, t)h(−,t) is an embedding for all ttt.

2) Specifically, knot complements can be homotopy equivalent without the knots being equivalent. Even if one requires the complements to be homeomorphic, it is a deep theorem of Gordon-Luecke that the knots must be equivalent.

My gut feeling is that this kind of thing is not possible: knot theory is simply not a homotopy invariant subject!
subject: homotopy knots?

content:
#4 There’s a little bit more going on here: the pair (C,S1×S1)(C, S^1\times S^1)(C,S1×S1) is a 3-manifold with boundary. The right homotopical approximation to a manifold is a “Poincare complex”, i.e., a homotopy type which “has Poincare duality”. Likewise the right homotopical approximation to a manifold with boundary is a “relative Poincare complex”. So you maybe you can add that to the mix.

Even with this, I would agree with Richard that there is not much likelyhood of getting an equivalence between knots and homotopy knots. Especially since surgery doesn’t work in dimension 3 at all, so the usual ways of turning homotopy theoretic information into results about manifolds won’t work here.
subject: homotopy knots?

content:
#5 @David, yeah, one thing to think about is to add more conditions on fff. On the other hand, there is already the strong condition that it does form a homotopy pushout to give S3S^3S3. This implies a lot. The question is: How much, if anything, does one have to require in addition?

@Richard: Yes, the first thought that comes to mind is that homotopy of knot embedding maps is clearly much coarser than isotopy. But then, the definition of “homotopy knots” above does not in fact involve homotopy of knot embeddings, instead it involves conditions on the knot complements. Maybe this is still too coarse, but it does not seem to be as obvious.

In either case, what I’d hope to see is some concrete arguments about how ϕ\phiϕ fails to be a bijection. If it’s not injective, can we produce a concrete example of a pair of knots that get send to the same “homotopy knot”-data?
subject: homotopy knots?

content: #6 Hi again Urs, this was what I intended to answer in 2). Just take the square knot and granny knot for example: homotopy equivalent complements, not equivalent as knots.

content: #7 For prime knots and CCC a 1-type it is injective I think, though this is a serious theorem.

#8 I agree that some knots have equivalent complements, and that the square knot and granny knot is the simplest such example. However, the type of maps S1×S1→K(G,1)S^1\times S^1 \to K(G,1)S1×S1→K(G,1) might have many connected components. That is to say, there might be many non-homotopic maps from the torus to the complement of the square/granny knot. Richard, are you claiming that not only their complements are the same, but also their boundary inclusions S1×S1→K(G,1)S^1\times S^1 \to K(G,1)S1×S1→K(G,1)?

I would also be curious to know whether or not the conditions in HomotopyKnot\mathbf{HomotopyKnot}HomotopyKnot already imply that the complement C is a 111-type.

#10 Egbert, I don’t think CCC will be forced to be a 1-type. To see this, it’s enough to have a map f ⁣:S1×S1→Df\colon S^1\times S^1\to Df:S1×S1→D so that the homotopy pushout of fff along pr1 ⁣:S1×S1→S1\mathrm{pr}_1\colon S^1\times S^1\to S^1pr1​:S1×S1→S1 is contractible. Then then take C:=S3∨DC:= S^3\vee DC:=S3∨D with the map S1×S1→fD→CS^1\times S^1\xrightarrow{f} D\to CS1×S1f​D→C.

I claim such a map fff exists with D=S2∨S1D=S^2\vee S^1D=S2∨S1. Decompose the torus as a union T1∪T2T_1\cup T_2T1​∪T2​ of two tubes along boundary circles (so that pr1\mathrm{pr}_1pr1​ projects each tube to a semicircle inside S1S^1S1). Define fff so that it sends the boundary circles to the basepoint of DDD, sends T1T_1T1​ surjectively to S2⊂DS^2\subset DS2⊂D by an obvious quotient map, and sends T2T_2T2​ to S1⊂DS^1\subset DS1⊂D by pr2\mathrm{pr}_2pr2​. The fundamental group and homology groups of the pushout of fff along pr1\mathrm{pr}_1pr1​ are calculated to be trivial.

The homotopy pushout S1⊔S1×S1DS^1\sqcup^{S^1\times S^1} DS1⊔S1×S1D is then contractible by the pasting lemma of pushouts:

S1→1↓↓S1×S1→D↓↓S1→1\begin{matrix}& S^1 & \rightarrow & 1 & \\ & \downarrow & & \downarrow & \\ & S^1\times S^1 & \rightarrow & D & \\ & \downarrow & & \downarrow & \\ & S^1 & \rightarrow & 1 \end{matrix}​S1↓S1×S1↓S1​→→→​1↓D↓1​​

because the vertical composite on the left is just the identity. Thank you for this nice example!

content: #14 It’s a good question. My guess is that, yes, it is a counterexample, but I do not off the top of my head have a proof. For links with more than one component there will definitely be counterexamples, because these are not necessarily determined by their complements even up to homeomorphism.
